title: Trump admin points fingers on FAA ground stop — and ends up implicating the GOP | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

The Trump administration has responded to arare and chaotic full ground stopat the nation’s airports by complaining about how Congress hasn’t fully funded the administration’s Federal Aviation Administration modernization efforts.

But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and President Donald Trump have struck their fellow Republicans, who still hold congressional majorities, with some friendly fire in the process.

Duffy and company have blamed the catastrophe on an outdated system that they inherited from the Biden administration and decades of predecessors, as they have after a series of other air traffic problems and disasters over the last two years that they’ve been in power. And there’s no question that the systemhas been outdated for some time.

But in citing a lack of full funding from Congress as the reason for the system’s continued failures, they’re implicating their own party.

What’s more, it’s pretty clear the administration has created some of its own problems on that front.

Duffy and Mullin began pointing the finger at Congress at a press conference late Friday night, hours after the ground stop began. Congress has given the Trump administration more than $14 billion for FAA modernization since Trump returned to the presidency — most of it ($12.5 billion) in his big agenda bill in June 2025. But the secretaries cast it as insufficient.

“Our air traffic control system is outdated,” Mullin said. “And it hasn’t been a priority for Congress. And so this is what happens when Congress kicks the can down the road.”

Added Duffy: “How many times does this have to happen before Congress gives the money to fix it?”

Soon, though, a reporter noted that Trump has been in office for nearly two years and that Republicans have majorities in both chambers.

Duffy responded that “often times you need a bipartisan vote.” House Speaker Mike Johnson has also cited the supposed lack of support from Democrats.

That’s usually a plausible defense. Having majorities doesn’t mean the party in power gets to pass whatever they want. Democrats can still block legislation using the filibuster’s 60-vote threshold in the Senate.

But when congressional Republicans passed that $12.5 billion in Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” in the summer of 2025, they actuallydidn’tneedany Democratic votes (and they didn’t get any).

Republicans passed it through the budget reconciliation process, which allows certain things to pass on party-line votes that aren’t subject to the filibuster.

But the bill didn’t include all the funding the administration sought. Duffy and the administration repeatedly referred to the $12.5 billion as a “down payment,” withanother $20 billion due later.

When asked about the Trump agenda bill Sunday on Fox News, GOP Rep. Nick Langworthy of New York signaled it should have included all of the FAA modernization money.

“Well, this is something that I have personally called for,” Langworthy said, adding, “I said we should fund this in full, up front.”

Conservative radio host Todd Starnesadded Sunday on X: “The broader question is why the Republican-controlled Congress refused Duffy’s full funding requests to modernize the FAA.”

In the 17 months since Trump signed the law, there has been little in the way of a push for Congress to pass more — either from the GOP majorities or from the president. And there are increasing questions about how that money is being allocated.

After Duffy’s and Mullin’s comments Friday night, Democrats said that the administrationhad only spent $1 billion of the $12.5 billion— and that it hasn’t even said where $8 billion of it will be spent.

(The Transportation Department has said the actual spending figure is higher than that. And Duffy told CNN’s Dana Bash on Sunday that “we are on track to have all of that $12.5 billion spent and deployed by the end of 2028.”)

Democrats also pointed to how Trump’s agenda bill included $75 billion for Immigration and Customs Enforcement — much of which remains unspent. Democrats argue that Republicans could have used some of that money for FAA modernization and that Congress could shift that funding now.

Democratic Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii, for example, said that “we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars.”

The administration also doesn’t seem to have been clear in documenting the needs and uses for more money.

The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office ina September reportsaid the administration had “not developed a comprehensive and well-documented lifecycle cost estimate for” its modernization work. It said the FAA was “unable to provide the analysis that supported” its numbers.

And that lack of explanation seems to remain a problem. While the administration last year initially requested around $20 billion more after the supposed “down payment,” that numberrose to $30 billion in late September. And right after the ground stop Friday, Duffy raised it to $50 billion — but without detailing where the extra money would go.

Even some Republicans seem to be pointing the finger back at the administration.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Monday that Congress needs “some explanations” from Duffy — who’s set to attend the Senate GOP’s weekly lunch meeting on Tuesday — as to why $8 billion of the approximately $12.5 billion hasn’t been designated.

“I mean, there’s some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is,” Thune said.

“I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the No. 1 priority. But also, we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we’re using taxpayer dollars wisely and well. So, we’ll hear them out,” he added.

And in the House, GOP Rep. Tom Emmer also defended Congress’ appropriations.

“I also listened to your clip from our friend, Secretary Mullin,” Emmertold Fox Newson Saturday. “I would argue that Congresshasbeen making this a priority.”

The Minnesota Republican added later that “Congress is going to need to have the details of what exactly that $50 billion is for.”

GOP Rep. Darrell Issa of California also said on Fox that “you need to actually ask the question of what are you going to use it for, how is it going to make us safer and more resilient.”

The other problem with the administration’s argument is it hasn’t been consistent in its push for more funding.

While it’s true that Duffy pushed for more, even right after the “One Big Beautiful Bill” passed and consistently since then, Trump at the time seemed to suggest the money was sufficient. The president said shortly before the bill passed that it would “modernize this decrepit relic and give America the best, most advanced air traffic control system on Earth — the best by far.”

Trump has also rarely mentioned the issue in recent months, only making a couple references to the air traffic control modernization issue this year, according to the Roll CallFactba.sedatabase of Trump’s comments.

Trump also didn’t weigh in publicly on the ground stop until Sunday, two days after it took place.

“If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” Trumpposted to social mediaon Sunday. He added: “We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve.”

But when it comes to why Congress hasn’t approved all of it, there’s plenty of blame to go around.

“I can’t apologize for what was passed off to us,” Duffy said Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

“And I can’t blame Republicans or Democrats, because it’s all of them.”

This story has been updated with additional developments.
